OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $r\geq 2$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ be such that $A_i\not\subseteq A_j$ for all $i\neq j$ and for any $t$ if there exists some $i$ with $\lvert A_i\rvert=t$ then there must exist at least $r$ sets of that size.
How large must $n$ be (as a function of $r$) to ensure that there is such a family which achieves $n-3$ distinct sizes of sets?
#776: [Er81i][Gu83]
combinatorics
A problem of Erdős and Trotter. For $r=1$ and $n>3$ the maximum possible is $n-2$. For $r>1$ and $n$ sufficiently large $n-3$ is achievable, but $n-2$ is never achievable.
Let $n_0(r)$ be such that whenever $n>n_0(r)$ there exists such a family with $n-3$ distinct set sizes. He and Tang [HeTa26b] (with ChatGPT) have proved that $n_0(2)=3$, $n_0(3)=8$, and for all $r\geq 4$\[2r+2\leq n_0(r)\leq 2r+2\log_2r+O(\log\log r),\]and hence $n_0(r)\sim 2r$ as $r\to \infty$.

 Thank you, Zach. This is a very good question, which generalizes the original Erdős--Trotter problem. For integers $\delta\ge 3$ and $r\ge 2$, we define\[
n_{0}^{(\delta)}(r):=\min\Bigl\{n_0:\ \forall\,n>n_0,\ g(n,r)\ge n-\delta\Bigr\}.
\]Then one can obtain the following conclusions (proofs can be found in this note):
1. If $\delta\ge 5$, then \(n_{0}^{(\delta)}(r)=O(\sqrt r)=o(r)\). In particular, the constant $C_{\delta}$ in your conjecture is $+\infty$.
2. When $\delta=4$, one can get a partial result: \(n_{0}^{(4)}(r) \ge \lceil \frac{r + 3}{3} \rceil\) for $r\geq 12$. Therefore, the constant $C_{4}$ in your conjecture lies in the interval $[1/2,\,3]$.
EDIT: I don't have a good guess for the specific value of $C_4$ at the moment, but I'm happy to hear your thoughts and discuss it further.

 Quanyu, this seems directly relevant to your comment about whether $n_0(r)=2r+C$ for a constant $C\in\{2,3,4\}$.
In an AI-conducted, computer-checked investigation, we obtain the following exact result:\[
g(27,11)=23,\qquad n_0(11)=27=2\cdot11+5.
\]First, any 11-multiplicity antichain on $[27]$ using at least 24 distinct sizes would have to use exactly the levels $2,3,\ldots,25$. Levels 0 and 27 cannot occur. If level 1 occurred, 11 singleton members would force every other member to avoid those 11 points, so all members would have size at most 16 and at most 16 levels could occur. Applying complementation similarly excludes level 26. After trimming to exactly 11 sets on each occupied level, the only possible 24-level profile is therefore $f_i=11$ for $2\leq i\leq25$.
The main tool is the classical prescribed-profile squashing theorem of Clements and Daykin--Godfrey--Hilton, together with Kruskal--Katona. If $f_i$ is a prescribed level profile, define\[
m_s=f_s,\qquad
m_i=f_i+\partial_{i+1}(m_{i+1}),
\]where $\partial_k(m)$ is the Kruskal--Katona minimum-shadow function. An
antichain with profile $(f_i)$ exists if and only if\[
m_i\leq \binom{n}{i}
\]at every level. https://github.com/mthiim/erdos_776/blob/main/docs/TECHNICAL_NOTE.md includes a short self-contained proof.
For $n=27$, with $f_i=11$ for $2\leq i\leq25$, the recurrence gives\[
m_2=352>351=\binom{27}{2}.
\]Thus no 24-level witness exists. On the other hand, the profile $f_i=11$ for $2\leq i\leq24$ satisfies every capacity inequality (with $m_2=327$). The colex construction gives an explicit family of 253 sets, and a separate bit-mask checker verifies directly that no two distinct sets are comparable. Hence $g(27,11)=23$.
For the threshold statement, the full profile on $[28]$ is feasible; the colex construction gives an explicit 275-set witness, again checked directly. We also construct a core antichain on 16 points with 11 sets of every size
$2,\ldots,13$. It has 88 free 12-sets, of which only 11 are needed. A two-point padding lemma grows a core with parameters $(q,s)$ to one with parameters $(q+2,s+1)$, while an elementary core-to-full construction uses these padded cores for both $n=28+2t$ and $n=29+2t$. This supplies a full-profile witness for every $n\geq28$, and therefore $n_0(11)=27$.
Exploratory computations suggest\[
n_0(r)=2r+5\qquad (r\geq11),
\]but this has not been proven!
Any comments/scrutiny much appreciated. The preliminary note, code, explicit witnesses, and one-command verification are available here: https://github.com/mthiim/erdos_776/

A partial proof 
claimed by Gilad Ronen (using OpenAI Codex (initial draft); Hermes Agent / gpt-5.6-sol (audit and verifier hardening)).
 Summary:
 This proves the exact threshold n_0(4)=12. Nonexistence at n=12 follows by classifying four sets on the two extreme levels; removing forced centres reduces the middle levels to four finite antichain assertions on seven points, the last also checked exhaustively. Explicit witnesses cover 13<=n<=19. For n>=20 the He--Tang label construction applies: with k=floor(n/2) and m minimal such that C(m,floor(m/2))>=k, the inequality C(k-5,2)>=k for k>=10 gives m<=k-5, its required room condition.
 Notes:
 Submitted as a partial result for r=4, not as a claim to settle Problem 776 in full. This is not a novelty or priority claim: proof claim #78 (17 July 2026) already states a broader exact theorem implying n_0(4)=12. The immutable commit includes explicit witnesses, strict verifiers (including under Python -O), an exhaustive checker, SAT search code, a publication manifest, and an audit record.

A full proof 
claimed by AI's operated by M.Thiim (using All ideas and lean formalization due to LLM's - exact contribution of each is specified in submission package. LLM's used: OpenAI ChatGPT 5.6 Pro, Anthropic Claude Fable 5, OpenAI Codex w gpt-5.6-Sol-Max).
 Summary:
 Erdős #776 asks when subsets of $[n]$ can occupy $n-3$ sizes, with no set contained in another and at least $r$ sets at each occupied size. Let $n_0(r)$ be the least $N$ working for every $n>N$. We prove $n_0(r)=2r+4$ for $4\le r\le10$ and $n_0(r)=2r+5$ for $r\ge11$.
Combining with $n_0(2)=3$ and $n_0(3)=8$, due to Yixin He and Quanyu Tang (as discussed in forum), this completes the table for $r\ge2$ with exact proven values.
Kruskal--Katona gives exact shadow constraints between successive size levels. For $r\ge11$, lower-level estimates and a four-level obstruction give a carry $1\le e\le6$. Here $e\ge1$ rules out $n=2r+5$, while $e\le6$ yields a feasible core; puncturing and repeated two-point padding then construct examples for every larger $n$. The cases $4\le r\le10$ use exact finite checks of the same constraints and constructions.
Lean proves the full set-family theorem for $r\ge4$; only three bounded ranges use finite evaluation, through proved soundness bridges.
 Notes:
 Whole proof package can be found on Github. This includes a README.md that serves as a useful entropy pint for the problem statement, links to paper, notes that can be useful to validating the proof and the lean formalization: https://github.com/mthiim/erdos_776/.
